The target is imbalanced: about 76% of people earn <=50K and 24% earn >50K, which is why a **stratified** split and **weighted** metrics are used (and why accuracy alone is misleading: always predicting <=50K already gives ~76%). The subsample contains some duplicate rows (inherent to the census data). Among numeric features, education level, age, hours per week and capital gain are the ones that vary most with income; the correlations between numeric features are weak, so multicollinearity is not a major concern for Logistic Regression.

Gradient Boosting ranks first (accuracy ≈ 85.8%, F1 ≈ 0.852, AUC ≈ 0.919), followed by SVC and Random Forest; the gaps between ranks 2–8 are small (≈ 1–2 points of F1). The test set has 1,600 rows, so differences below ≈ 1 point are within noise. **Gaussian Naive Bayes collapses (accuracy ≈ 31.8%, AUC ≈ 0.59)**: after one-hot encoding, dozens of binary columns are strongly dependent, breaking its independence/Gaussian assumptions, and it over-predicts the >50K class. The single Decision Tree is next-worst (AUC ≈ 0.74) because it overfits; its ensembles (Bagging, Random Forest) fix much of that.

Because of the 76/24 imbalance, Precision, Recall and F1 (weighted) are all dominated by the majority class and track accuracy closely. ROC-AUC is the most discriminating metric here: boosting/SVC/Logistic reach ≈ 0.90–0.92, KNN and the single tree are noticeably lower. Naive Bayes is the clear outlier on every metric except weighted precision.

Tuning gains are measured by **5-fold CV on the training set**. They are small on this dataset: Random Forest +0.011 (max_depth=20 helps), KNN +0.007 (k=21, manhattan), AdaBoost +0.006, and ≈ 0 for Gradient Boosting, SVC, MLP and Logistic Regression — the default settings were already near the ceiling of what these features can support. Differences this small should not be over-interpreted; the tuned models are essentially tied.

> ✏️ **DRAFT observation — verify against your plots and rewrite in your own words (course rule 7.5: interpretation must be original).**

**Gradient Boosting (200 trees, depth 3, learning rate 0.1)** is selected because it has the highest CV weighted-F1 on training data (selection never touches the test set); it scores ≈ 85.9% accuracy / F1 ≈ 0.854 / AUC ≈ 0.921 on the held-out test set. The confusion matrix shows the main weakness: recall for the >50K class is only ≈ 0.61 (precision ≈ 0.76), i.e. about 4 in 10 high earners are missed. If the application cared more about finding high earners, we would lower the decision threshold or use class weights. Trade-off: boosting is less interpretable than Logistic Regression but clearly better than a single tree, and trains in seconds on this size.

Inertia drops steeply until k≈5–6 (389 → 295 → 205 → 168 → 134) and then flattens (117 at k=7), so the elbow lies around 5–6. The silhouette score peaks at **k=6 (≈ 0.428)**, with k=5 (0.417) and k=7 (0.417) almost as good. We use k=6 (max silhouette); k=5 is a defensible alternative. A silhouette ≈ 0.43 indicates reasonably well-separated, moderately compact clusters.

> ✏️ **DRAFT observation — verify against your plots and rewrite in your own words (course rule 7.5: interpretation must be original).**

**Ward** gives the best silhouette (≈ 0.420) and Calinski-Harabasz (≈ 128) with balanced sizes (45/45/39/28/22/21). Single linkage chains: one cluster of 193 points and five tiny ones (silhouette < 0). Note the trap: single linkage has the *lowest* (best-looking) Davies-Bouldin (≈ 0.64) even though the clustering is useless, because tiny outlier clusters have tiny scatter. Always read the three metrics together.

K-Means is slightly ahead of Ward on all three internal metrics (Silhouette 0.428 vs 0.420, Davies-Bouldin 0.825 vs 0.852 — lower is better, Calinski-Harabasz 135.1 vs 128.0). The differences are small; K-Means optimises within-cluster variance directly, which is what these metrics reward. Both produce 6 clusters of similar size.

The first two principal components explain ≈ 78% of the variance (PC1 ≈ 44%, PC2 ≈ 33%), so the 2-D view is reliable. Both algorithms recover six visually distinct groups; the boundaries of the Ward clusters are slightly more irregular than K-Means' Voronoi-style cells. The right-hand panel (coloured by gender) shows no spatial pattern, confirming gender does not drive the segments.

> ✏️ **DRAFT observation — verify against your plots and rewrite in your own words (course rule 7.5: interpretation must be original).**

There is no ground-truth label, so validation is by agreement and interpretation: K-Means and Ward agree strongly (ARI ≈ 0.89, NMI ≈ 0.90). The profile table gives business-meaningful segments, e.g. **high income / high spending** (cluster 3, avg age ≈ 33 — prime target), **high income / low spending** (cluster 2, ≈ 42 — under-engaged, worth targeting), **low income / high spending** (cluster 4, ≈ 25), **low income / low spending** (cluster 5, ≈ 46), and two mid-income groups separated by age (≈ 27 vs ≈ 56). Gender mix is close to 40–60% in every cluster, so gender is not a segmentation driver.
